papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models: Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting in large language models? Specifically, does the model merely mimic exemplars, what changes occur in the projection space (logits), and does CoT enable deeper and broader utilization of pre-trained knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This work analyzes the internal mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting, finding that LLMs imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with question understanding, exhibit fluctuating but ultimately more concentrated logits distributions, and activate a broader set of neurons in final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought prompting enhances LLM reasoning by guiding models to imitate exemplar formats, focus logits distributions, and activate a broader set of knowledge-related neurons, leading to more accurate and confident answers.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs imitate the format of CoT exemplars (e.g., using sequence words like 'first', 'then') while generating personalized responses based on their understanding of the question.
During CoT generation, token logits fluctuate more than with standard prompts, but the final answer generation shows a more concentrated logits distribution, suggesting clearer direction.
CoT prompts lead to a broader range and higher intensity of neuron activations in the final layers compared to standard prompts, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval from pre-training.
Successful imitation of transferred CoT prompts correlates with higher answer accuracy, suggesting that understanding the exemplar format is key to CoT's effectiveness.
The probability distribution over candidate answers at the answer generation step is more concentrated (lower entropy) under CoT prompting, indicating higher model confidence in the selected answer.
papers.limitation: Experiments were conducted on a limited sample of 50 test examples per dataset due to budget constraints.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more models and tasks.
Explore the dynamic changes in neuron activations across different layers.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models, with numerous studies exploring factors influencing its performance. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. To further demystify the operational principles, this work examines three key aspects: decoding, projection, and activation, aiming to elucidate the changes that occur within models when employing Chainof-Thought. Our findings reveal that LLMs effectively imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with their understanding of the question, exhibiting fluctuations in token logits during generation but ultimately producing a more concentrated logits distribution, and activating a broader set of neurons in the final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval compared to standard prompts. Our code and data will be publicly avialable when the paper is accepted.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Language Mixing in Reasoning Language Models: Patterns, Impact, and Internal Causes
papers.research_question: What are the patterns, performance impact, and internal causes of language mixing (reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt) in Reasoning Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of language mixing in Reasoning Language Models, showing it reflects latent internal processing preferences (a bias towards Latin and Han scripts) and that controlling the reasoning script via constrained decoding can significantly improve multilingual reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Language mixing in RLMs is a systematic behavior tied to the models' internal language preferences; controlling the reasoning script based on these preferences offers a practical way to optimize multilingual reasoning performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Language mixing is most prevalent when the input language is neither English nor Chinese, suggesting these serve as internal pivot languages.
The degree of language mixing increases with task difficulty and is more pronounced in STEM subjects.
Distillation amplifies language mixing compared to the base backbone models.
Forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy for non-Latin/Han-script input languages.
The script composition of reasoning traces closely mirrors that of the model's internal representations (analyzed via Logit Lens), indicating language mixing reflects latent processing preferences.
papers.limitation: Analysis focuses on valid reasoning traces that conclude with a final answer, excluding cases of endless reasoning.
future_direction: Controlling and adapting the reasoning language to build more robust, interpretable, and user-aligned RLMs.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models (RLMs) excel at complex tasks by leveraging a chain-of-thought process to generate structured intermediate steps. However, language mixing, i.e., reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt, has been observed in their outputs and shown to affect performance, though its impact remains debated. We present the first systematic study of language mixing in RLMs, examining its patterns, impact, and internal causes across 15 languages, 7 task difficulty levels, and 18 subject areas, and show how all three factors influence language mixing. Moreover, we demonstrate that the choice of reasoning language significantly affects performance: forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy. Finally, we show that the script composition of reasoning traces closely aligns with that of the model's internal representations, indicating that language mixing reflects latent processing preferences in RLMs. Our findings provide actionable insights for optimizing multilingual reasoning and open new directions for controlling reasoning languages to build more interpretable and adaptable RLMs.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Tracing the Traces: Latent Temporal Signals for Efficient and Accurate Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning models improve their problem-solving ability through inference-time scaling, allocating more compute via longer token budgets. Identifying which reasoning traces are likely to succeed remains a key opportunity: reliably predicting productive paths can substantially reduce wasted computation and improve overall efficiency. We introduce Latent-Trajectory signals that characterize the temporal evolution of a model's internal representations during the generation of intermediate reasoning tokens. By measuring the overall change in latent representations between the start and end of reasoning, the change accumulated across intermediate steps, and the extent to which these changes advance toward the final state, we show that these signals predict solution accuracy more reliably than both cross-layer metrics and output-based confidence measures. When used to guide answer selection across multiple sampled generations, Latent-Trajectory signals make test-time scaling more effective and efficient than majority voting, reducing token usage by up to 70% while preserving and even improving accuracy by 2.6% on average. Moreover, these predictive signals often emerge early in the reasoning trace, enabling early selection and allocation of compute to the most promising candidates. Our findings contribute not only practical strategies for inference-time efficiency, but also a deeper interpretability perspective on how reasoning processes are represented and differentiated in latent space.

papers.title: Interpreting Context Look-ups in Transformers: Investigating Attention-MLP Interactions
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly, providing a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads process context and use next-token neurons to help predict a word associated with, but not previously seen in that context, providing insight into how attention heads can work with MLP neurons to predict new words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can recognize contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron.
An automated method can explain and characterize interactions between attention heads and token-predicting neurons.
The head explanation score can be used to evaluate the quality of explanations.
The phenomenon is observed across different model families and sizes (GPT-2 and Pythia variants).
Ablation experiments confirm that the identified attention heads are causally involved in predicting the token.
papers.limitation:
Focus on max-activating behavior of neurons, which might overlook subtler activation patterns.
Reliance on a maximum of 30 prompts per neuron.
GPT-4 struggles with longer prompts and may generate poor explanations for certain patterns (like induction-style prompts).
Scope limited to neurons whose associated tokens are whole words and prompts shorter than 100 tokens.
future_direction: Investigate whether this phenomenon happens to such neurons throughout their range of activations.
Look into whether multiple attention heads could work with a single next-token neuron.
Look into whether a single attention head could work with multiple next-token neurons.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for advancing their theoretical foundations and real-world applications. While the attention mechanism and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have been studied independently, their interactions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates how attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words. We propose a methodology to identify next-token neurons, find prompts that highly activate them, and determine the upstream attention heads responsible. We then generate and evaluate explanations for the activity of these attention heads in an automated manner. Our findings reveal that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly. This mechanism provides a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction. Our approach offers a foundation for further research into the intricate workings of LLMs and their impact on text generation and understanding.

papers.title: Systematic Generalization and Emergent Structures in Transformers Trained on Structured Tasks
papers.research_question: How and when can transformers acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization on algorithmic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Two-layer causal transformers with label-based order encoding can learn algorithmic tasks and generalize to longer sequences, exhibiting signs of task decomposition and shared computation across tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve structured algorithmic tasks and generalize systematically, with attention layers developing task decomposition and shared computation.
papers.key_findings:
Label-based order encoding enables strong length generalization in transformers on algorithmic tasks.
Two-layer transformers are sufficient to solve multi-level sorting tasks, while single-layer models fail.
Attention patterns in two-layer models show task decomposition: first layer attends to items in the same feature group, second layer attends to the next output token.
In multi-task learning, transformers can learn multiple tasks simultaneously and generalize to longer sequences, with attention heads showing shared computation across tasks.
Task-conditioned item representations are reorganized according to the task structure, showing clustering by relevant features.
papers.limitation:
Label-based encoding alone would not represent true item distance information.
The tasks are simple and synthetic, and may not capture the complexity of natural data.
future_direction: Explore learning and generalization dynamics in transformer-based agents to understand the acquisition of task-conditioned, multi-level behavioral policies in structured environments.
Characterize the degree of possible computational modularity in multi-headed attention in relation to task structures.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks have seen great success in natural language processing and machine vision, where task objectives such as next word prediction and image classification benefit from nuanced context sensitivity across high-dimensional inputs. However, there is an ongoing debate about how and when transformers can acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization. Here, we explore how well a causal transformer can perform a set of algorithmic tasks, including copying, sorting, and hierarchical compositions of these operations. We demonstrate strong generalization to sequences longer than those used in training by replacing the standard positional encoding typically used in transformers with labels arbitrarily paired with items in the sequence. We search for the layer and head configuration sufficient to solve these tasks, then probe for signs of systematic processing in latent representations and attention patterns. We show that two-layer transformers learn reliable solutions to multi-level problems, develop signs of task decomposition, and encode input items in a way that encourages the exploitation of shared computation across related tasks. These results provide key insights into how attention layers support structured computation both within a task and across multiple tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: ThoughtProbe: Classifier-Guided LLM Thought Space Exploration via Probing Representations
papers.research_question: How can we use hidden representations of LLMs as discriminative signals to guide tree-structured exploration of reasoning paths and improve reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThoughtProbe, an inference-time framework that uses a classifier trained on hidden representations to guide tree-structured exploration of reasoning paths, improving reasoning performance without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ThoughtProbe is an effective inference-time framework that leverages hidden reasoning features to improve reasoning performance without requiring expensive fine-tuning or elaborate prompting strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden representations of LLMs can effectively discriminate between CoT and non-CoT responses.
The classifier's logit can be used as a scoring mechanism to rank reasoning paths.
ThoughtProbe outperforms existing inference-time methods on multiple reasoning benchmarks.
Different LLMs encode CoT features in different representation types and layers.
Branch-aggregation selection outperforms best-of-N selection.
papers.limitation:
Fixed token lengths for node expansion may disrupt natural reasoning.
Gap between coverage and accuracy suggests room for improvement in answer selection.
Increased inference-time cost due to tree expansion and classifier evaluation.
future_direction: Explore more flexible, semantic-aware splitting criteria for node expansion.
Develop more sophisticated scoring metrics and aggregation methods for answer selection.
Reduce computational overhead via more efficient pruning, early stopping, or lightweight scoring.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces ThoughtProbe, a novel inference time framework that leverages the hidden reasoning features of Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve their reasoning performance. Unlike previous works that manipulate the hidden representations to steer LLM generation, we harness them as discriminative signals to guide the tree structured response space exploration. In each node expansion, a classifier serves as a scoring and ranking mechanism that efficiently allocates computational resources by prioritizing higher score candidates for continuation. After completing the tree expansion, we collect answers from all branches to form a candidate answer pool. We then propose a branch aggregation method that marginalizes over all supporting branches by aggregating their CoT scores, thereby identifying the optimal answer from the pool. Experimental results show that our framework's comprehensive exploration not only covers valid reasoning chains but also effectively identifies them, achieving significant improvements across multiple arithmetic reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
papers.research_question: Which reasoning steps (sentences) in a chain-of-thought are important for guiding the reasoning trajectory and final answer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sentence-level analysis methods (black-box resampling and white-box attention analysis) to identify 'thought anchors'—critical reasoning steps that guide the trajectory of chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Sentence-level analysis provides a promising intermediate abstraction for understanding reasoning in LLMs, with methods converging to identify critical 'thought anchor' steps that structure the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
Plan generation and uncertainty management sentences have higher counterfactual importance than active computation or fact retrieval sentences.
Specialized 'receiver' attention heads consistently attend to thought anchor sentences, providing a mechanistic correlate of importance.
Sentence-sentence causal graphs reveal that stronger close-range links and weaker long-range links correlate with higher reasoning accuracy, especially in mathematical domains.
papers.limitation: The counterfactual importance metric can yield high-variance estimates when the number of semantically divergent resampled sentences is low.
future_direction: Investigating adaptive scales for defining reasoning steps beyond fixed sentences.
Further work on the limitations of the counterfactual importance metric with limited data.
papers.abstract: Current frontier large-language models rely on reasoning to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Many existing interpretability are limited in this area, as standard methods have been designed to study single forward passes of a model rather than the multi-token computational steps that unfold during reasoning. We argue that analyzing reasoning traces at the sentence level is a promising approach to understanding reasoning processes. We introduce a black-box method that measures each sentence's counterfactual importance by repeatedly sampling replacement sentences from the model, filtering for semantically different ones, and continuing the chain of thought from that point onwards to quantify the sentence's impact on the distribution of final answers. We discover that certain sentences can have an outsized impact on the trajectory of the reasoning trace and final answer. We term these sentences \textit{thought anchors}. These are generally planning or uncertainty management sentences, and specialized attention heads consistently attend from subsequent sentences to thought anchors. We further show that examining sentence-sentence causal links within a reasoning trace gives insight into a model's behavior. Such information can be used to predict a problem's difficulty and the extent different question domains involve sequential or diffuse reasoning. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate that our techniques together provide a practical toolkit for analyzing reasoning models by conducting a detailed case study of how the model solves a difficult math problem, finding that our techniques yield a consistent picture of the reasoning trace's structure. We provide an open-source tool (thought-anchors.com) for visualizing the outputs of our methods on further problems. The convergence across our methods shows the potential of sentence-level analysis for a deeper understanding of reasoning models.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: A Statistical Physics of Language Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we model and understand the continuous-time reasoning dynamics of transformer language models using a statistical physics framework?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a statistical physics framework using stochastic differential equations and a Switching Linear Dynamical System to model and simulate reasoning dynamics in language models, enabling the prediction of misaligned states and failure modes.
papers.conclusion: The SLDS framework provides a tractable and interpretable model for reasoning dynamics, offering tools to study and predict critical transitions such as misaligned states in language models.
papers.key_findings:
A rank-40 projection captures 50% of the variance in sentence-level hidden state trajectories.
Four latent reasoning regimes are identified through Gaussian Mixture Model clustering of residuals.
The SLDS model accurately predicts reasoning dynamics and outperforms single-regime linear models in one-step-ahead prediction.
The framework shows transferability across models and tasks, though performance degrades across different model architectures.
In a case study, the SLDS successfully models and predicts adversarially induced belief shifts, demonstrating its utility for failure mode analysis.
future_direction: Future work could explore learning more invariant reasoning representations for better generalization.
papers.abstract: Transformer LMs show emergent reasoning that resists mechanistic understanding. We offer a statistical physics framework for continuous-time chain-of-thought reasoning dynamics. We model sentence-level hidden state trajectories as a stochastic dynamical system on a lower-dimensional manifold. This drift-diffusion system uses latent regime switching to capture diverse reasoning phases, including misaligned states or failures. Empirical trajectories (8 models, 7 benchmarks) show a rank-40 projection (balancing variance capture and feasibility) explains ~50% variance. We find four latent reasoning regimes. An SLDS model is formulated and validated to capture these features. The framework enables low-cost reasoning simulation, offering tools to study and predict critical transitions like misaligned states or other LM failures.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Exploring and Exploiting the Inherent Efficiency within Large Reasoning Models for Self-Guided Efficiency Enhancement
papers.research_question: Can the inherent efficiency within large reasoning models be exploited to reduce overthinking and enhance reasoning efficiency without compromising performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that large reasoning models inherently possess untapped efficiency potential, and proposes two self-guided methods—Efficiency Steering (a training-free activation steering technique) and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL (a reinforcement learning framework)—that significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance.
papers.conclusion: Overthinking in large reasoning models is a controllable behavior embedded in internal representations; the proposed self-guided methods (Efficiency Steering and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL) successfully enhance reasoning efficiency without external supervision, offering practical directions for building more cost-efficient reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LRMs exhibit inherent efficiency: the shortest correct reasoning paths are often less than half the length of the longest correct ones, indicating substantial untapped efficiency potential.
Efficient and verbose reasoning paths are linearly separable in the model's representation space, with consistent positional shifts across layers and difficulty levels.
Efficiency Steering, a training-free method that injects a single vector direction derived from contrastive reasoning pairs, can controllably modulate reasoning length without compromising accuracy.
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, which uses a dynamic reward function balancing correctness and brevity, significantly reduces reasoning length while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy across multiple benchmarks.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on simpler mathematical problems (Levels 1-3) leads to efficient reasoning that transfers well to harder problems, suggesting that efficiency priors learned from simple data are effective.
papers.limitation:
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL is sensitive to optimization steps; beyond 30 steps, efficiency improves but correctness can deteriorate, indicating a trade-off that requires careful tuning.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on harder mathematical examples (Levels 4-5) does not yield as favorable efficiency outcomes as training on simpler examples, suggesting that data distribution impacts the method's effectiveness.
future_direction: Further exploration of representational properties of LLMs to build efficiency-aware alignment strategies with minimal external supervision.
Investigating curriculum-aware or simplicity-biased training strategies for self-rewarded efficiency optimization, as simpler problems may provide better efficiency outcomes at lower training cost.
Refining the capabilities that already exist within LRMs for building more efficient and accessible reasoning systems.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced language models' capabilities in complex problem-solving by emulating human-like deliberative thinking. However, these models often exhibit overthinking (i.e., the generation of unnecessarily verbose and redundant content), which hinders efficiency and inflates inference cost. In this work, we explore the representational and behavioral origins of this inefficiency, revealing that LRMs inherently possess the capacity for more concise reasoning. Empirical analyses show that correct reasoning paths vary significantly in length, and the shortest correct responses often suffice, indicating untapped efficiency potential. Exploiting these findings, we propose two lightweight methods to enhance LRM efficiency. First, we introduce Efficiency Steering, a training-free activation steering technique that modulates reasoning behavior via a single direction in the model's representation space. Second, we develop Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically balances task accuracy and brevity by rewarding concise correct solutions. Extensive experiments on seven LRM backbones across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our methods significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance. Our results highlight that reasoning efficiency can be improved by leveraging and guiding the intrinsic capabilities of existing models in a self-guided manner.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: Humanlike Cognitive Patterns as Emergent Phenomena in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of LLMs' emergent cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity, comparing them to human benchmarks and highlighting partial alignment, advancements in advanced models, and potential for collaboration.
papers.conclusion: The review synthesizes evidence that LLMs partially replicate human cognitive patterns, with notable advancements in reasoning and creativity, but limitations remain, indicating the need for further research in memory, attention, and open-source model development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate several human-like decision-making biases but lack others such as reflection effect and waste aversion.
Advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short.
LLMs show strong analogical reasoning abilities, sometimes surpassing human performance.
In creativity, LLMs excel in language-based tasks but struggle with divergent thinking requiring real-world context.
LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators to augment human creativity in problem-solving settings.
papers.limitation:
Over-reliance on GPT family models and insufficient testing of open-source LLMs, leading to potential bias and non-replication.
Memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs have not been sufficiently studied compared to decision-making, reasoning, and creativity.
future_direction: Study memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs
Increase testing and use of open-source LLMs
Adopt practices using multiple models in experiments
papers.abstract: Research on emergent patterns in Large Language Models (LLMs) has gained significant traction in both psychology and artificial intelligence, motivating the need for a comprehensive review that offers a synthesis of this complex landscape. In this article, we systematically review LLMs' capabilities across three important cognitive domains: decision-making biases, reasoning, and creativity. We use empirical studies drawing on established psychological tests and compare LLMs' performance to human benchmarks. On decision-making, our synthesis reveals that while LLMs demonstrate several human-like biases, some biases observed in humans are absent, indicating cognitive patterns that only partially align with human decision-making. On reasoning, advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short of human-level performance. A distinct dichotomy emerges in creativity: while LLMs excel in language-based creative tasks, such as storytelling, they struggle with divergent thinking tasks that require real-world context. Nonetheless, studies suggest that LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators, augmenting creativity in human-machine problem-solving settings. Discussing key limitations, we also offer guidance for future research in areas such as memory, attention, and open-source model development.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Eliciting Chain-of-Thought in Base LLMs via Gradient-Based Representation Optimization
papers.research_question: Can we solely manipulate the hidden states to elicit CoT reasoning from a base LLM, without distorting its language quality?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a gradient-based hidden state optimization method to elicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning in base LLMs, using a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework to guide hidden states toward reasoning while preserving language quality.
papers.conclusion: Presents a principled gradient-based activation optimization method to elicit CoT reasoning from base LLMs, grounded in probabilistic generation theory, which balances likelihood and prior terms to activate reasoning without distribution shift, and consistently outperforms vector arithmetic methods.
papers.key_findings:
Our method consistently outperforms existing hidden state steering methods across diverse reasoning benchmarks.
The method unlocks latent reasoning capabilities in base LLMs without additional training.
The optimization framework balances reasoning effectiveness and linguistic fluency.
The method is effective across multiple LLM architectures (Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, Phi).
The method's performance depends on the choice of hidden states and layers, with middle layers showing better classification performance.
papers.limitation:
The method can only unlock intrinsic reasoning abilities and cannot inject new capabilities; for models with limited intrinsic reasoning capacity, it cannot create non-existent capabilities.
The method's effectiveness depends on the classification performance and layer selection; improper choices may lead to suboptimal results.
future_direction: Integrating the method with post-training techniques to further amplify reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is a critical capability for large language models (LLMs), enabling them to tackle com- plex multi-step tasks. While base LLMs, pre-trained on general text corpora, often struggle with reasoning due to a lack of specialized training, recent studies reveal their latent reason- ing potential tied to hidden states. However, existing hidden state manipulation methods, such as linear activation steering, suffer from limitations due to their rigid and unconstrained nature, often leading to distribution shifts and degraded text quality. In this work, we propose a novel approach for elic- iting CoT reasoning from base LLMs through hidden state manipulation grounded in probabilistic conditional generation. By reformulating the challenge as an optimization problem with a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework, our method guides hidden states toward reasoning-oriented trajectories while preserving linguistic coherence. Extensive evaluations across mathematical, commonsense, and logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our approach con- sistently outperforms existing steering methods, offering a theoretically principled and effective solution for enhancing reasoning capabilities in base LLMs.

papers.title: Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning in LLMs: An Exploration Using Cognitive Dual-System Theory
papers.research_question: How can the contributions of knowledge retrieval and reasoning adjustment be separated and quantified in large language models during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cognition attribution framework based on dual-system theory to decouple knowledge and reasoning in LLMs, revealing domain-specific reasoning benefits, scaling effects, and a hierarchical separation of knowledge (lower layers) and reasoning (higher layers).
papers.conclusion: The proposed cognition attribution architecture offers a novel perspective for understanding LLM cognition and provides insights into scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and the reasoning limitations of small models.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, chemistry) and potentially impairing knowledge-intensive domains.
Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Scaling also makes reasoning significantly more prudent (reduces overthinking) and modestly more intelligent (increases correction) in specific domains.
Knowledge retrieval primarily occurs in lower network layers, while reasoning adjustments are localized in higher layers, suggesting a functional separation.
Small LLMs tend to overthink more than they correct during reasoning, leading to negative or limited reasoning gains.
LLMs exhibit a human-like anchoring effect, which reasoning adjustment helps to mitigate.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice QA; future work should extend to open-ended generation.
The study does not include ultra-large models (>100B parameters).
The methods are simplified and may not fully capture the underlying mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to open-ended generation tasks.
Include ultra-large models (>100B parameters) in the study.
Conduct a more in-depth exploration of the phenomena observed using the framework.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) leverage both knowledge and reasoning during inference, the capacity to distinguish between them plays a pivotal role in model analysis, interpretability, and development. Inspired by dual-system cognitive theory, we propose a cognition attribution framework to decouple the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. In particular, the cognition of LLMs is decomposed into two distinct yet complementary phases: knowledge retrieval (Phase 1) and reasoning adjustment (Phase 2). To separate these phases, LLMs are prompted to generate answers under two different cognitive modes, fast thinking and slow thinking, respectively. The performance under different cognitive modes is analyzed to quantify the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. This architecture is employed to 15 LLMs across 3 datasets. Results reveal: (1) reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, and chemistry) and potentially imparing knowledge-intensive domains. (2) Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Additionally, parameter scaling make LLMs reasoning significantly more prudent, while moderately more intelligent. (3) Knowledge primarily resides in lower network layers, while reasoning operates in higher layers. Our framework not only helps understand LLMs from a "decoupling" perspective, but also provides new insights into existing research, including scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and limitations of small-model reasoning.

papers.title: Attention over learned object embeddings enables complex visual\n reasoning
papers.research_question: Can a neural-network-based approach combining learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning achieve state-of-the-art performance on complex visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components?
papers.core_contribution: The Aloe model, which combines learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning, achieves state-of-the-art performance on three visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components, demonstrating that flexibility and performance need not be traded off.
papers.conclusion: The success of Aloe suggests that with the right soft biases and learning objectives—object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning—neural networks can achieve strong performance on spatiotemporal reasoning tasks without resorting to task-specific modular components.
papers.key_findings:
Aloe outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on CLEVRER, CATER, and ACRE across various question and reasoning types.
The combination of object-level discretization, global self-attention, and self-supervised learning is crucial for strong performance; ablations of any component lead to significant drops.
Aloe is data-efficient, matching previous SOTA performance on CLEVRER with only 50-60% of the training data.
The model generalizes across three distinct visual reasoning tasks (CLEVRER, CATER, ACRE) without any architectural modifications.
Qualitative analysis of attention weights shows the model aligns objects across time and focuses on relevant objects and words for answering questions.
papers.limitation:
Applied only to synthetic datasets due to a lack of real-world datasets testing higher-order spatiotemporal reasoning.
The domains used may not fully evaluate the intended capacities due to hidden biases or other factors.
May perpetuate biases found in training data and could invite problematic applications involving automated assignment of blame.
future_direction: Applying the approach to real-world datasets, such as the upcoming Traffic QA.
Investigating other self-supervised losses and masking schemes to further improve dynamics learning.
Designing and developing more challenging tasks that better approximate human-level visual, spatiotemporal, and causal reasoning.
papers.abstract:
Neural networks have achieved success in a wide array of perceptual tasks but
often fail at tasks involving both perception and higher-level reasoning. On
these more challenging tasks, bespoke approaches (such as modular symbolic
components, independent dynamics models or semantic parsers) targeted towards
that specific type of task have typically performed better. The downside to
these targeted approaches, however, is that they can be more brittle than
general-purpose neural networks, requiring significant modification or even
redesign according to the particular task at hand. Here, we propose a more
general neural-network-based approach to dynamic visual reasoning problems that
obtains state-of-the-art performance on three different domains, in each case
outperforming bespoke modular approaches tailored specifically to the task. Our
method relies on learned object-centric representations, self-attention and
self-supervised dynamics learning, and all three elements together are required
for strong performance to emerge. The success of this combination suggests that
there may be no need to trade off flexibility for performance on problems
involving spatio-temporal or causal-style reasoning. With the right soft biases
and learning objectives in a neural network we may be able to attain the best
of both worlds.

papers.title: ThinkLess: A Training-Free Inference-Efficient Method for Reducing Reasoning Redundancy
papers.abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves reasoning in large language models (LLMs), the excessive length of reasoning tokens increases latency and KV cache memory usage, and may even truncate final answers under context limits. We propose ThinkLess, an inference-efficient framework that terminates reasoning generation early and maintains output quality without modifying the model. Atttention analysis reveals that answer tokens focus minimally on earlier reasoning steps and primarily attend to the reasoning terminator token, due to information migration under causal masking. Building on this insight, ThinkLess inserts the terminator token at earlier positions to skip redundant reasoning while preserving the underlying knowledge transfer. To prevent format discruption casued by early termination, ThinkLess employs a lightweight post-regulation mechanism, relying on the model's natural instruction-following ability to produce well-structured answers. Without fine-tuning or auxiliary data, ThinkLess achieves comparable accuracy to full-length CoT decoding while greatly reducing decoding time and memory consumption.

papers.title: Semantic Composition in Visually Grounded Language Models
papers.research_question: This thesis explores whether and how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces multiple methods (WinogroundVQA, Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, Causal Tracing, Syntactic MeanPool, Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization) to probe, analyze, and improve the compositional abilities of visually grounded language models.
papers.conclusion: The work explores the compositionality of visually grounded semantics, introducing methods to probe and improve it, and draws connections to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.
papers.key_findings:
Generative vision-language models like BLIP 2.0 and MiniGPT-4 perform poorly on the compositional WinogroundVQA benchmark.
Syntactic Neural Module Distillation reveals that larger sentence embedding models (GTR-T5) are more compositional, but model size is not the only determining factor.
Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization (CACR) improves relation alignment in vision-language models and outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method (IAIS) on the Winoground benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, hyperparameter tuning for the SynNaMoN experiments was unfeasible, and the dataset had to be constrained to a subset of trees and production rules.
The choice of linguistic formalism (Penn Treebank) may influence the probing results of compositional structure.
future_direction: Exploring whether different linguistic formalisms are better proxies for a model's compositional structure.
Further work on the causal tracing experiment for image captioning models (implementation in progress).
papers.abstract: What is sentence meaning and its ideal representation? Much of the expressive power of human language derives from semantic composition, the mind's ability to represent meaning hierarchically & relationally over constituents. At the same time, much sentential meaning is outside the text and requires grounding in sensory, motor, and experiential modalities to be adequately learned. Although large language models display considerable compositional ability, recent work shows that visually-grounded language models drastically fail to represent compositional structure. In this thesis, we explore whether & how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so. Specifically, we introduce 1) WinogroundVQA, a new compositional visual question answering benchmark, 2) Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, a measure of compositional ability in sentence embedding models, 3) Causal Tracing for Image Captioning Models to locate neural representations vital for vision-language composition, 4) Syntactic MeanPool to inject a compositional inductive bias into sentence embeddings, and 5) Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization, a self-supervised objective function for vision-language relation alignment. We close by discussing connections of our work to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
Faithfulness depends on model size and task difficulty, with easier tasks and larger models leading to less faithful reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground truth about the model's internal reasoning process, making it impossible to know if CoT is truly faithful.
Analysis limited to RLHF-finetuned models; faithfulness may differ for pretrained LLMs or other training schemes.
future_direction: Investigate training schemes different from RLHF for eliciting more faithful reasoning.
Use the proposed metrics to increase the faithfulness of CoT and build systems with trustworthy reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

papers.title: LaDiR: Latent Diffusion Enhances LLMs for Text Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can latent diffusion models enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, particularly by enabling self-correction and refinement at semantic levels?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LaDiR, a reasoning framework that uses a VAE to encode reasoning steps into latent thought tokens and a latent diffusion model to iteratively denoise them, enabling semantic-level refinement and diverse reasoning trajectories.
papers.conclusion: LaDiR establishes a new paradigm for text reasoning with latent diffusion, balancing accuracy and diversity, and revealing the potential of continuous latent representations for enhancing LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LaDiR outperforms existing autoregressive, diffusion-based, and latent reasoning methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving higher Pass@1 and Pass@100 accuracy.
On code generation benchmarks, LaDiR achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly on challenging datasets like HumanEval+.
On the Countdown planning task, LaDiR shows significant improvements in both Pass@1 and Pass@100, demonstrating enhanced planning ability and diversity.
The method provides interpretable latent reasoning steps that can be decoded into human-readable text.
LaDiR offers a flexible trade-off between accuracy and test-time compute through iterative denoising steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate their reasoning ability through chain-of-thought (CoT) generation.
